summary: This informational RFC presents real-world measurements, taken in August 2014 and June 2015, of how often packets with IPv6 Extension Headers get dropped in the Internet and where. The results serve as a problem statement for operational advice on filtering such packets.

eli5.summary: Some network gear throws away IPv6 packets with extra add-ons. This reports how often and where it happens.

subtitle: Widespread Internet filtering of IPv6 packets with extension headers

tldr.problem: IPv6 Extension Headers, which are essential for features like fragmentation and IPv6 routing headers, are being dropped by a significant percentage of Internet infrastructure, but the extent and location of this dropping is not well documented.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC presents real-world measurements from August 2014 and June 2015, probing thousands of public IPv6 servers with packets containing destination options, hop-by-hop options, and fragment headers to measure drop rates and identify which networks are dropping them.
tldr.outcome: The results show that 10-54% of packets with extension headers are dropped depending on the header type and server type, with significant drops occurring at transit networks outside the destination operator's control.

today: RFC 7872 remains an important reference for understanding IPv6 operability challenges. The problem identified in 2014-2015 has motivated research into solutions such as more lenient filtering policies, better operator guidance, and protocol designs that work around the dropping of extension headers. However, the fundamental issue—that a significant portion of the Internet cannot reliably handle IPv6 Extension Headers—persists.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Extension Headers Matter
sections.content:
IPv6 Extension Headers (EHs) are a core part of the IPv6 protocol specification. They allow the protocol to be extended and provide essential functionality such as IPv6 fragmentation, source routing, and hop-by-hop options. However, there has been suspicion that these headers are being dropped in real networks, though concrete data has been scarce.

This RFC presents the first comprehensive real-world measurements of the extent to which packets with IPv6 EHs are actually dropped in the Internet. The measurements were conducted in August 2014 and again in June 2015, with similar results. Understanding this problem is crucial because if IPv6 EHs cannot reliably traverse the Internet, it limits what applications and protocols can do with IPv6.
sections.eli5: IPv6 packets can have extra headers that add features like splitting into smaller pieces. But routers might throw away these packets, which breaks things.

sections.title: Measurement Methodology and Results
sections.content:
The researchers compiled lists of public IPv6 servers from two sources: the "World IPv6 Launch" initiative and Alexa's Top 1-Million Web Sites, obtaining IPv6 addresses (AAAA records) for web servers, mail servers, and DNS nameservers. Three types of probe packets were sent to each server: IPv6 packets with a Destination Options header of 8 bytes, IPv6 packets resulting in two IPv6 fragments of 512 bytes each, and IPv6 packets with a Hop-by-Hop Options header of 8 bytes. All probes used TCP to appropriate service ports.

The results were sobering. For web servers on the World IPv6 Launch dataset, 11.88% of packets with Destination Options headers were dropped, 40.70% with Hop-by-Hop headers, and 30.51% with Fragment headers. For mail servers, drop rates were even higher: 17.07%, 48.86%, and 39.17% respectively. Nameserver packet drop rates ranged from 15.37% to 43.25%. The Alexa Top 1M Sites dataset showed similar or worse results, with Hop-by-Hop header drop rates reaching 54.12% on nameservers.
sections.eli5: Researchers sent different types of special packets to thousands of Internet servers. Between 10% and 55% of packets with special headers were never delivered, depending on the header type and server type.

sections.title: Where Packets Are Being Dropped
sections.content: A critical finding is that many packets are being dropped not at the destination network but at transit networks along the path. The RFC distinguishes between best-case and worst-case scenarios due to ambiguity in assigning dropped packets to specific Autonomous Systems (ASes). For Destination Options headers on web servers, 17.60% to 20.80% of drops occurred in transit networks. For Hop-by-Hop headers, this was 31.43% to 40%. For fragment headers on web servers, 5.08% to 6.78% of drops were in transit. This is significant because destination operators can control their own equipment, but drops in transit networks affect deployments outside the operator's control.
sections.eli5: Often packets are dropped by networks between the sender and destination, not by the destination itself.

sections.title: What This Means for IPv6 Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC makes two key observations. First, it challenges the assumption that primarily IPv6 fragments are being dropped: the data show that IPv6 Extension Headers in general cause problems. Second, the significant percentage of drops occurring in transit ASes reveals that the problem is not under the control of destination networks.

These results create a problem statement for the Internet community. IPv6 features that rely on extension headers cannot be reliably deployed when so much infrastructure silently drops them. Applications and protocols built on IPv6 cannot depend on extension headers working, even though the IPv6 specification defines them as a core feature. This limits IPv6's ability to evolve and support new functionality.
sections.eli5: Because so many networks throw away these packets, programmers cannot rely on them working. This makes it hard for IPv6 to add new features.

sections.title: Reproducing and Troubleshooting the Problem
sections.content:
The RFC includes detailed appendices explaining exactly how to reproduce the experiments and troubleshoot IPv6 extension header problems. The measurement methodology uses standard UNIX tools and the SI6 Networks IPv6 Toolkit, making it possible for other researchers and operators to validate and extend the results.

For troubleshooting, the RFC recommends using IPv6 traceroute with and without extension headers to identify which node in the path is dropping packets. The last node responding to EH-enabled traceroute helps locate the dropping device. The RFC provides tools and techniques for this isolation process, along with guidance on how to identify which organization operates the dropping network.
sections.eli5: The document explains step-by-step how to find where your packets are being dropped so you can report it or fix it.
